description: We are a team from the Antalya local event. We build Last Breath at Shackleton, a story-driven Unity game where NASA's retired spacecraft on the Moon and Mars tell their own stories at the lunar south pole. Our interests: game development, space exploration, NASA mission history and science storytelling for students. The game and presentation are available in Turkish and English. Skills we use and welcome: Unity/C#, 3D design, writing and education.
summary: Last Breath at Shackleton is a story-driven Unity survival game set at the lunar south pole, where NASA's retired spacecraft tell their own stories. Players have 30 minutes of oxygen to repair a base, complete six science missions and explore. Along the way they reach the real impact sites of Lunar Prospector (1999) and LCROSS (2009) and unlock a Heritage Archive in which 12 NASA machines on the Moon and Mars, from Surveyor 3 and Apollo 11's Eagle to Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity, speak in the first person: why they were sent, what they discovered and why they were left behind. Every fact is checked against NASA's NSSDCA catalogue and NASA Science mission pages, and fictional elements are clearly labelled. The water ice that those missions found becomes water and oxygen in the player's greenhouse, so past discoveries literally keep you alive. The game is free, works offline and is available in Turkish and English, aimed at students aged 10-16. It turns discarded hardware from "space junk" into a memorable story about how exploration builds on what came before.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Last Breath at Shackleton is a third-person survival and storytelling game set near Shackleton crater at the lunar south pole. The player is an astronaut with a 30-minute oxygen budget. To survive, they restore station power, revive the solar panels, repair suit damage with the right tool, collect soil and ice samples (measuring hydrogen before concluding there is ice), fix a science device and antenna, grow plants in a greenhouse and return to the airlock in time.

HOW IT TELLS THE STORY OF DISCARDED EQUIPMENT

- Real impact sites: the map contains memorials at the places where NASA deliberately ended two missions at the south pole: Lunar Prospector (31 July 1999) and LCROSS with its Centaur upper stage (9 October 2009, Cabeus crater). Reaching a site unlocks that spacecraft's story.

- Heritage Archive: a terminal at the base holds 12 NASA machines left on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 "Eagle" descent stage, the ALSEP stations, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Lunar Prospector and LCROSS on the Moon; Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity on Mars. Each entry is written in the first person (why it was sent, what it found, why it stayed behind) with a separate science panel and its NASA source. Reading pauses the oxygen clock.

- Discoveries keep you alive: the water ice confirmed by LCROSS becomes water and oxygen in the player's greenhouse, inspired by NASA's Veggie system on the ISS.

- A late-game event: a fictional retired satellite (RELAY-7) crashes into a crater and injures crewmate Roger. The player must choose whether to share oxygen to rescue him. The game then links this moment to the real, intentional impacts of Lunar Prospector and LCROSS.

- The debrief shows missions completed, decisions made, and how many heritage stories were found and read.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

The project turns "space junk" into a story of exploration. It is aimed at students aged 10-16, science clubs and outreach events. It is free, runs offline on a standard PC, and is fully bilingual (Turkish and English, switchable with one key), so it can be used in classrooms in Turkey and abroad. Facts come from NASA sources; fictional characters and objects are clearly labelled in the game and in the presentation.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Unity 6 (URP), C#, the Unity Input System, Blender (model conversion). A procedural editor script builds the whole map (crater terrain, habitat, greenhouse, impact sites, archive terminal, hazard zones). Lunar gravity (1.62 m/s2) is used for movement. NASA 3D Resources models (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Habitat Demonstration Unit) are used in the scene. An automated screenshot tool captures the same scenes in both languages for the presentation.

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

Instead of a list of facts, each machine has its own voice, and the player physically visits where missions ended. We kept historical accuracy (dates and end-of-mission facts from NSSDCA), separated fiction from fact, respected NASA branding rules, and disclosed our use of AI tools.

STATUS AND NEXT STEPS

Playable Windows prototype in Turkish and English. Next: playable Mars sites (Spirit, Opportunity, InSight), real south-pole terrain from NASA elevation data, a WebGL browser version, a teacher mode and voice-over for archive stories.
